'''bivocalized''' (bī-vō′kạl-īzd), ''a.'' Placed between two vowels.

'''bivouac''' (biv′ọ̈-ak), ''n.'' [Also ''bivouack'', in 18th century occasionally ''biouac, biovac, bihovac'', < F. ''bivouac'', formerly ''biouac'', orig. ''bivac'', prob. < G. dial. (Swiss) ''beiwacht'', a patrol of citizens added in time of alarm or commotion to the regular town watch (cf. G. ''beiwache'', a keeping watch), < ''bei'', = E. ''by'', + *''wacht'', G. ''wache'' = E. ''watch'', ''n.''] An encampment of soldiers in the open air without tents, each soldier remaining dressed and with his weapons by him; hence, figuratively, a position or situation of readiness for emergencies, or a situation demanding extreme watchfulness.
{{smaller block|We followed up our victory until night overtook us about two miles from Port Gibson; then the troops went into ''bivouac'' for the night.
{{right|''U. S. Grant'', Personal Memoirs, I. 484.}}
<poem>In the world’s broad field of battle,
  In the ''bivouac'' of Life,
Be not like dumb, driven cattle!
  Be a hero in the strife!</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Psalm of Life.}}}}

'''bivouac''' (biv′ọ̈-ak), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''bivouacked'', ppr. ''bivouacking''. [< ''bivouac'', ''n.''] To encamp in the open air without tents or covering, as soldiers on a march or in expectation

'''biza''', ''n.'' See ''bisa.''

'''bizard†''' (biz′ärd), ''n.'' Same as ''bizarre.''

'''bizarre''' (bi-zär′), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [F. (formerly also ''bigearre'', ''bijarre''), strange, capricious, formerly headlong, angry, orig. valiant, = It. ''bizzarro'', irascible, choleric, < Sp. Pg. ''bizarro'', gallant, brave, valiant, perhaps < Basque ''bizarra'', a beard; cf. Sp. ''hombre de bigote'', a man of spirit (''bigote'', mustache).] '''I.''' ''a.'' Odd; fanciful; fantastical; whimsical; grotesque.
{{smaller block|Although he was very grave in his own person, he loved the most ''bizarr'' and irregular wits.
{{right|''Roger North'', Life of Lord Guilford, i. 117.}}
Matter and Motions are ''bizarr'' things, humoursome and capricious to excess. ''Gentleman Instructed'', p. 559.

These paintings . . . depended from the walls not only in their main surfaces, but in very many nooks which the ''bizarre'' architecture of the chateau rendered necessary.
{{right|''Poe'', Tales, I. 366.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A variety of carnation in which the white ground-color is striped with two colors, one darker than the other.

'''bizarrerie''' (bi-zä′re-ri), ''n.'' [< F. ''bizarrerie'', < ''bizarre.''] Bizarre quality.

{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}

'''blab<sup>2</sup>†''' (blab), ''n.'' [Another form of ''bleb'', ''blob''.] A bubble; a blister; a swelling.

'''blab<sup>2</sup>†''' (blab), ''v. i.'' or ''t.'' [< ''blab''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''] To swell out or up; make swollen, as the cheeks.

'''blabber<sup>1</sup>†''' (blab′ėr), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''blaberen'', stammer, talk without reason, blabber, blab, = LG. ''blabbern'' = G. ''plappern'', blab, babble, = Dan. ''blabbre'', blabber, gabble: imitative words, prob. in part of independent origin. Similar forms of imitative origin are Sw. dial. ''bladdra'', ''blaffra'', prattle, D. LG. G. ''blaffen'' (> E. ''blaff''), yelp; OHG. ''blabbizōn'', MHG. ''blepzen'', babble; ML. ''blaberare'', for L. ''blaterare'', babble; Gael. ''blabaran'', a stammerer, ''blabhdach'', babbling, ''plabair'', a babbler; E. ''blather'', ''blether''<sup>1</sup>, ''babble'', etc.] '''1.''' To speak inarticulately; babble; mumble.
{{smaller block|Now you may see how easie it is to speak right, and not to ''blabber'' like boors in any speech.
{{right|''Wodroephe'', Fr. and Eng. Gram. (1623), p. 126.}}}}
'''2.''' To tell tales; blab; talk idly.—'''3.''' To fib; falter. ''Skinner.''—'''4.''' To whistle to a horse. ''Skinner.''

'''blabber<sup>1</sup>''' (blab′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''blabber''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] A tattler; a telltale.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis fairies’ treasure,
Which but reveal’d, brings on the ''blabber’s'' ruin.</poem>
{{right|''Massinger and Field'', Fatal Dowry, iv. 1.}}}}

'''blabbering†''' (blab′ėr-ing), ''a.'' Inarticulate; babbling.

'''blabber-lipped†''' (blab′ėr-lipt), ''a.'' [< ME. ''blabyrlypped'', also ''blabberlipped:'' see ''blabber<sup>2</sup>'' and ''blubber-lipped.''] Having swollen or protruding lips; blubber-lipped.

See ''earth''.—'''Black Flags,''' bands of irregular soldiers infesting the upper valley of the Red River in Tonquin. They were originally survivors of the Taiping rebellion in China; increased by the accession of various adventurers, they fought against the French in their wars with Annam, about 1873–85.—'''Black Friday, frost,''' etc. See the nouns.—'''Black glass,''' a glass made in Venice of sand, sulphur, and peroxid of manganese. It is of a deep-black color.—'''Black hagden.''' See ''hagden''.—'''Black Hand,''' an anarchistic society in Spain composed of members of the laboring classes. Many of its members in southern Spain were arrested and imprisoned in 1883.—'''Black Harry, Black Will,''' local names in the United States of the sea-bass, ''Centropristes furvus''.—'''Black herring.''' See ''herring''.—'''Black in the flesh,''' and '''waxed and black in the grain,''' terms applied to skins curried on the inner and outer sides respectively. The former is applied to the uppers of men’s shoes, and the latter of women’s.—'''Black japan.''' See ''japan''.—'''Black Maria,''' a closely covered vehicle, usually painted black, used in conveying prisoners to and from jail.—'''Black martin, Monday, naphtha, ocher,''' etc. See the nouns.—'''Black rent,''' exactions formerly levied by native chieftains in Ireland, particularly upon districts where English were settled.

'''biwa'''<sup>2</sup> (bē′wạ̈), ''n.''   [Jap., = Chinese ''pi-pa'', a guitar.]   A Japanese musical instrument with four strings, resembling a flat mandolin.

'''biweekly''' (bī-wēk′li), ''a.'' and ''adv.''   [< ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> + ''weekly.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Occurring or appearing every two weeks: as, a ''biweekly'' magazine. {{smaller|Sometimes erroneously used in place of ''semiweekly'', for or occurring twice in a week.}}

'''II.''' ''adv.'' Fortnightly.

'''biwepe†''', ''v.'' An obsolete form of ''beweep.''

'''Bixaceæ''' (bik-sā′sẹ̄-ē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Bixa'', the typical genus, + ''-aceæ.'']   A natural order of polypetalous exogenous plants, nearly related to the ''Violaceæ.'' {{smaller|They are mostly shrubs or trees, natives of the warmer regions of the globe, and of little economic importance. The orange-coloring principle (C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>26</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) of arnotto, a vermilion-red powder, insoluble in water or ether, but soluble in alcohol and benzol.—'''2.''' A variety of arnotto, having from six to ten times the coloring power of common arnotto, from quicker extraction.

'''bjelkite''' (biel′kīt), ''n.''   [< ''Bjelke'' (see def.) + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.]   A variety of the mineral cosalite from the Bjelke mine, Nordmark, Sweden.

'''bk., bks.''' Abbreviations of ''book, books.''

'''B. L.''' An abbreviation (''a'') of ''Bachelor of Law;'' (''b'') in ''com.'', of ''bill of lading.''

'''blab<sup>1</sup>''' (blab), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''blabbed'', ppr. ''blabbing.''   [In ME. only in the freq. form (which is preferred for such words; cf. ''babble, gabble, gabber, jabber'', etc.), but the derived noun ''blabbe'', a blab, telltale, occurs: see ''blab''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', and ''blabber''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To utter or tell in a thoughtless or unnecessary manner (what ought to be kept secret); let out (secrets).
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh, that delightful engine of her thoughts,
That ''blabb’d'' them with such pleasing eloquence.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Yonder a vile physician, ''blabbing''
The case of his patient.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, xxvii. 3.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To talk indiscreetly; tattle; tell tales.
{{smaller block|You’re sure the little milliner won’t ''blab?''
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|But letters, however carefully drilled to be circumspect, are sure to ''blab'', and those of Pope leave in the reader’s mind an unpleasant feeling of circumspection.
{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 427.}}}}

'''blab<sup>1</sup>''' (blab), ''n.''   [< ME. ''blabbe:'' see ''blab''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   A babbler; a telltale; one who betrays secrets, or tells things which ought to be kept secret.
{{smaller block|<poem>Good merchant, lay your fingers on your mouth;
Be not a ''blab.''</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', James IV., v.}}}}

All friendship, and avoided as a ''blab'',
The mark of fool set on his front!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 495.}}}}

'''black''' (blak), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ME. ''blak'', ''blek'', ''bleke'', < AS. ''blæc'' (in def. inflection ''blaca'', ''blace'', sometimes with long vowel ''blāca'', ''blāce'', and thus confused with ''blāc'', ''blǣc'', ME. ''blake'', etc., shining, white (see ''bleak<sup>1</sup>''), = OHG. (in comp.) ''blah'', ''blach''), black, = (with appar. diff. orig. suffix) Icel. ''blakkr'', dark, dusky, = Sw. ''black'', grayish, dark, = Dan. ''blak'', dark (whence the noun, AS. ''blæc'' = MLG. ''black'', LG. ''blak'' = MHG. ''black bletch'', ''bleach''<sup>2</sup>; but not connected, unless remotely, with ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>, ''bleach''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Possessing in the highest degree the property of absorbing light; reflecting and transmitting little or no light; of the color of soot or coal; of the darkest possible hue; sable; optically, wholly destitute of color, or absolutely dark, whether from the absence or from the total absorption of light: opposed to ''white.''
{{smaller block|I spy a ''black'', suspicious, threat’ning cloud.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., v. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>On either hand, as far as eye could see,
A great ''black'' swamp and of an evil smell.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}}
{{smaller block|A ''black'' body is one which absorbs every ray which falls on it. It can, therefore, neither reflect nor transmit. A mass of coke suggests the conception of such a body.
{{right|''Tait'', Light, § 307.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' Characterized by the absence of light; involved or enveloped in darkness.
{{smaller block|In the twilight, in the evening, in the ''black'' and dark night.
{{right|Prov. vii. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|And, beauty dead, ''black'' chaos comes again.
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 1020.}}}}
'''3.''' Dismal; gloomy; sullen and forbidding: as, a ''black'' prospect.—'''4.''' Destitute of moral light or goodness; evil; wicked; atrocious: as, ''black'' deeds.
{{smaller block|<poem>“Thou art,” quoth she, “a sea, a sovereign king,
And, lo, there falls into thy boundless flood
''Black'' lust, dishonour, shame, misgoverning.”</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 654.}}}}
{{smaller block|During stages in which maintenance of authority is most imperative, direct disloyalty is considered the ''blackest'' of crimes.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 532.}}}}
'''5.''' Calamitous; disastrous; bringing ruin or desolation: as, ''black'' tidings; ''black'' Friday.
{{smaller block|''Black'' tidings these, . . . ''blacker'' never came to New England.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Twice-Told Tales, II.}}}}
'''6.''' Deadly; malignant; baneful: as, a ''black'' augury.
{{smaller block|<poem>Taking thy part, hath rush’d aside the law,
And turned that ''black'' word death to banishment.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 3.}}}}
'''7.''' Clouded with anger; frowning; threatening; boding ill: as, ''black'' looks.
{{smaller block|<poem>She hath abated me of half my train;
Look’d ''black'' upon me; struck me with her tongue.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, ii. 4.}}}}
'''8.''' Wearing black or dark clothing, armor, etc.: as, Edward the ''Black'' Prince; ''black'' friars.—'''9.''' Stained with dirt; soiled; dirty: as, ''black'' hands. [Colloq.]—'''Black Act, Black acts.''' {{smaller|See ''act.''}}—'''Black amber.''' {{smaller|Same as ''jet.''}}—'''Black and blue,''' {{smaller|having the dark livid color of a bruise in the flesh, which is accompanied with a mixture of blue. See ''blue'' and ''blae.''}}
{{smaller block|Mistress Ford . . . is beaten ''black and blue'', that you cannot see a white spot about her.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iv. 5.}}}}
'''Black and tan,''' {{smaller|having black hair upon the back, and tan or yellowish-brown upon the face, flanks, and legs, as some dogs: said specifically of a kind of terrier dog, and sometimes used elliptically as a substantive.}}
{{smaller block|Consider the St. Bernards and the mastiffs, the pugs and the bull-dogs, the ''black-and-tans'' and the King Charlies.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXVIII. 599.}}}}
'''Black antimony, art, assembly, bead-tree, bearberry,''' {{smaller|etc. See under the nouns.}}—'''Black belt,''' {{smaller|that region of the southern United States, comprising portions of South Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, in which the ratio of the colored population to the white is greatest.}}—'''Black bile.''' {{smaller|See ''atrabile.''}}—'''Black bindweed, book, canker, chalk, death,''' etc. See the nouns.—'''Black drink,''' a decoction of the leaves of ''Ilex cassine'', used by the Indians of the southern United States as a medicine and as a drink of ceremony.—'''Black earth.''' See ''earth''.—'''Black Flags,''' bands of irregular soldiers infesting the upper valley of the Red River in Tonquin. They were originally survivors of the Taiping rebellion in China; increased by the accession of various adventurers, they fought against the French in their wars with Annam, about 1873–85.—'''Black Friday, frost,''' etc. See the nouns.—'''Black glass,''' a glass made in Venice of sand, sulphur, and peroxid of manganese. It is of a deep-black color.—'''Black hagden.''' See ''hagden''.—'''Black Hand,''' an anarchistic society in Spain composed of members of the laboring classes. Many of its members in southern Spain were arrested and imprisoned in 1883.—'''Black Harry, Black Will,''' local names in the United States of the sea-bass, ''Centropristes furvus''.—'''Black herring.''' See ''herring''.—'''Black in the flesh,''' and '''waxed and black in the grain,''' terms applied to skins curried on the inner and outer sides respectively. The former is applied to the uppers of men’s shoes, and the latter of women’s.—'''Black japan.''' See ''japan''.—'''Black Maria,''' a closely covered vehicle, usually painted black, used in conveying prisoners to and from jail.—'''Black martin, Monday, naphtha, ocher,''' etc. See the nouns.—'''Black rent,''' exactions formerly levied by native chieftains in Ireland, particularly upon districts where English were settled.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
